newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine shares plunge, analysts see no relief.
newsitem.headline: Philippine shares plunge, analysts see no relief.

text.p: Philippine shares took a savage dive on Tuesday in the bloodiest trading of the year, with the key index sinking to its lowest level in six months, and analysts said the worst might not be over.

Fears that property prices would crash, along with reports that foreign funds were staying away and lingering apprehensions about a rise in U.S. interest rates, reverberated across the board, sparing virtually no one.

The main index, skidding for the seventh straight day, plunged more than 100 points to a day's low of 2,887.37 before being rescued by short-covering which pushed it up to a close of 2,909.30, down 2.73 percent or 81.66 points on the day.
It was the biggest drop in the index since last October 29 when it sank to 2,904.41. It brought the index loss to a total of 313.68 points in the past week.
Losers swamped gainers 118 to 25 while 49 issues were unchanged.
"It's like a snowball rolling down a hill and getting bigger and bigger," Irving Ackerman, president of I. Ackerman & Co Inc, told Reuters.
"There was more bloodbath today than yesterday. Nobody was spared," said Monique Lecaros, trader at Sun Hung Kai Securities.
The assessment by Abacus Securities Corp was that the market would remain bearish possibly for another month, with sporadic rallies, analyst Vangie Yap said.
"Right now, everything is going down and people are afraid of pouring in money again because they don't know if the market has hit bottom already," Yap said.
Analysts said the downtrend could continue with a slower momentum when the market resumed trading on Thursday.
Philippine financial markets are closed on Wednesday for a holiday in honour of Filipino World War Two soldiers.
On Tuesday, even blue chips reeled, with only four companies out of the 30 firms making up the main index posting gains.

The four gainers were utility-based conglomerate Aboitiz Equity, cellular phone firm Piltel PS., property developer Ayala Land-B and Benpres Holdings which has interests in power generation and television.

"I haven't seen a day when we lost a hundred points recently. It was pretty bad today. I can't say when I have seen worse," Ackerman said. "Every time you looked at the board, it went down another five points."
Ackerman said there was only one bright point. "When this is over and the market turns around, there are going to be opportunities galore for making profits," he said.
Most property issues hit year-lows, buffeted by speculation that a glut in the sector would lead to a price crash.
The sell-off also battered banks on fears of their large loan exposures to the property sector.
Among those badly hit in the property sector were housing developer Empire East Land Holdings Inc and parent Megaworld Properties and Holdings Inc.
"It's an over-reaction. They are comparing us with Thailand, but I don't think there's over-building here at the moment," said Sun Hung Kai research director Raul Ruiz.
Reports that Thailand's financial sector was having financial problems sent the Thai bourse plunging last month to a near five-year low.
